opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of my favorite questions. The way I think about it, pre-training is where almost all of the actual knowledge and capability gets built. You're compressing an enormous amount of text, and to predict the next token well, the model has to build internal representations of a huge range of concepts: facts about the world, styles of writing, different personas, reasoning patterns, all of it. By the end of pre-training you have something like a vast library of latent capabilities and characters, but they aren't organized around being helpful to you specifically.

Post-training, at least in my view, is much less about teaching the model new things and much more about selection and elicitation. You're picking out which of those latent behaviors you want to surface and making them the default. When you do RLHF or instruction tuning on a relatively small amount of data and see a dramatic change in behavior, that tells you the capability was mostly already there. You're steering, not building from scratch.

That framing matters a lot from an interpretability perspective, because if post-training mostly reweights or reroutes existing representations, you should be able to see that inside the model. You can look at which features become more or less active, which circuits get amplified, and in principle you could get some of the same effects by intervening on those internals directly rather than going through a whole training run. It also cuts the other way for safety. If a behavior has been suppressed rather than removed, the underlying representations may still be sitting there, and that helps explain why jailbreaks work and why fine-tuning can sometimes undo safety training so easily.

It isn't purely elicitation, though. With newer reinforcement learning on reasoning tasks, there's a real question about how much is genuinely new capability versus sharpening things the base model could already do occasionally. My intuition is that it's still mostly sharpening, taking something that worked one time in a hundred and making it reliable, but that's exactly the kind of question I'd want to answer by looking inside the model instead of arguing about it from behavior alone.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training builds “almost all” of the model’s knowledge and capability and describes a large store of latent capabilities.

r002.rationale: It characterizes post-training as selecting and eliciting latent behaviors, making them more likely defaults, and says newer reinforcement learning mostly makes occasional abilities reliable.

r003.rationale: It discusses suppressed behaviors and safety, but does not say that instruction tuning in the earlier RLHF paradigm suppresses base-model capabilities through mode collapse.

r004.rationale: It describes reinforcement learning as sharpening abilities the base model could sometimes perform, but does not frame RL after instruction tuning as recovering capabilities learned during pre-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I've come to think about it is that pre-training is where basically all of the capability lives, and post-training is mostly about selection and access. When you train a model on a huge slice of the internet, it's not learning one personality or one way of doing things. It's learning to model an enormous distribution of writers, programmers, experts, novices, trolls, the whole range. All of those are latent in the weights. The pre-trained model is more like a simulator of many possible speakers than it is a single agent.

And then post-training, whether that's supervised fine-tuning or RLHF or whatever flavor you're using, is comparatively a very small amount of signal. We're talking orders of magnitude less data and compute than pre-training. So it's hard to argue it's teaching the model much that's genuinely new. What it's really doing is reshaping the prior. It's saying, out of all the characters you could be, be this one. Be the helpful, careful assistant rather than the Reddit commenter or the anonymous forum poster. It's narrowing the distribution and making certain behaviors much more probable and reliable.

The evidence for this view, I think, is that you can often get surprisingly far with very little post-training. A few thousand well-chosen examples can produce something that feels like a dramatically different model, and that only makes sense if the underlying behavior was already there and you just needed to point at it. The flip side is that if a capability isn't in the pre-trained model, post-training mostly can't conjure it. You can make a model more willing to attempt a task, more consistent in format, better at knowing when to refuse, but you're not going to teach it a whole new domain of reasoning with a few thousand examples.

Where it gets more interesting and more debatable is RL with verifiable rewards, the reasoning-style training that's become big. There I'd say the line blurs a bit, because you're letting the model generate its own experience and reinforcing trajectories that work. That looks more like actual learning than selection. But even there, my intuition is that the elicitation framing still mostly holds. You're reinforcing search strategies and chains of thought that were already reachable, just low probability, and making them the default. The model gets dramatically better at using what it knows, more than it learns new facts about the world.

So the practical consequence for people building these systems is that if you want a model to do something, the first question should be whether pre-training gave it the raw material. If it did, post-training is remarkably efficient at bringing it out. If it didn't, you're probably going to have a bad time trying to patch it in afterward, and the fix is upstream in the data mix.

r001.rationale: It says that “basically all” capability lives in pre-training and that post-training cannot add capabilities or facts that are absent from the pre-trained model.

r002.rationale: It describes post-training, including verifiable-reward RL, as making already reachable behaviors more probable and reliable rather than mainly adding new capabilities.

r003.rationale: It discusses narrowing behavior through post-training, but does not identify the earlier RLHF paradigm, instruction tuning, or mode collapse suppressing base-model capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says RL can reinforce already reachable strategies, but does not frame reinforcement learning after instruction tuning as recovering pre-training capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think of pre-training as building this enormous repertoire of capabilities and patterns, and post-training as shaping which parts of that repertoire the model actually uses when you interact with it. During pre-training, the model learns to predict text across all these different contexts. That requires learning facts, but also something about reasoning, communication, and how different kinds of people approach problems.

But being able to model a helpful answer isn’t the same as reliably giving a helpful answer. The pre-training objective doesn’t inherently privilege that over modeling a mistaken answer or continuing a fictional dialogue. Post-training gives the model a much stronger signal about what behavior we want in the assistant setting.

I wouldn’t draw an absolute boundary, though, where pre-training is all learning and post-training is just revealing what’s already there. Post-training can teach things, too. The interesting question is how much of an improvement comes from acquiring a new capability versus making an existing capability more reliable or easier to elicit. And just looking at better performance on a benchmark doesn’t necessarily tell you which of those happened.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training as building an “enormous repertoire” and says it teaches facts, reasoning, and communication, while post-training shapes how that repertoire is used.

r002.rationale: It says post-training can make existing capabilities more reliable or easier to elicit, but does not characterize reinforcement learning specifically or state that this is its primary effect.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss the earlier RLHF paradigm, instruction tuning suppressing base-model capabilities, or mode collapse.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe reinforcement learning after instruction tuning as recovering capabilities learned during pre-training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of pre-training as building this enormous repertoire of capabilities and patterns, and post-training as shaping which of those patterns the model actually uses in a conversation. During pre-training, it’s learning to predict text across a huge range of contexts. That includes useful reasoning, but also mistakes, contradictions, and lots of different ways of behaving. So learning a behavior and reliably choosing that behavior are different things.

Post-training helps establish that choice: when to answer directly, when to ask a clarifying question, how to follow instructions. And it can make capabilities that were hard to access much easier to elicit.

But I wouldn’t draw an absolute boundary where pre-training supplies all the knowledge and post-training only changes the presentation. Post-training is learning, too. It can teach the model something new. The interesting question is whether a particular improvement reflects a new capability or more reliable access to something the model could already do. Those can look very similar from the outside.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training builds a broad repertoire of capabilities and patterns, but does not establish that it supplies most of the model’s knowledge and capabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes post-training as making existing capabilities easier to elicit, but does not characterize reinforcement learning as primarily increasing the likelihood of already-possible outputs; it also says post-training can teach something new.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss the earlier RLHF paradigm, instruction tuning suppressing base-model capabilities, or mode collapse.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe reinforcement learning after instruction tuning as a way to recover pre-training capabilities.
